Hundredth
hun'dredth
a. and n. (the ordinal of a hundred; used to date the flood by Noah's own years, and to name the monthly interest Nehemiah made the nobles restore)
From hundred — Old English hundred, from hund, a hundred, and raed, a reckoning — with the ordinal ending. The Hebrew at Nehemiah 5:11 is literally meath ha-keseph, the hundredth of the money.

Biblical Definition

Two very different uses. Genesis dates the flood by the years of one man: “Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters was upon the earth” (Genesis 7:6), and the drying is dated “in the six hundredth and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month” (Genesis 8:13). Moses supplies day, month, and year throughout the account, which is not how legend is written. The other use is economic and is one of the sharpest scenes in the Old Testament. Nehemiah found that Jewish nobles were lending to their own brethren at interest during a famine and taking their fields, vineyards, and children in pledge. He assembled a great congregation against them and demanded restitution: “Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them” (Nehemiah 5:11). The hundredth part is generally understood as the monthly rate — one percent a month, twelve percent a year — and the law forbade any usury of a brother. They agreed, and Nehemiah took an oath of them (Nehemiah 5:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines hundredth as the ordinal of a hundred, and as a noun one of a hundred equal parts.

expand to see more

HUNDREDTH, a. The ordinal of a hundred.

HUNDRED, a. Denoting the product of ten multiplied by ten, or the number of ten times ten.

HUNDRED, n. A collection, consisting of ten times ten individuals or units.

USURY, n. Formerly, interest; or a premium given for the use of money.

2. In present usage, illegal interest; a premium or compensation paid for the use of money borrowed, beyond the rate of interest established by law.

Key Scripture

Genesis 7:6 — "And Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters was upon the earth."

Genesis 8:13 — "And it came to pass in the six hundredth and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried up from off the earth: and Noah removed the covering of the ark, and looked, and, behold, the face of the ground was dry."

Nehemiah 5:11 — "Restore, I pray you, to them, even this day, their lands, their vineyards, their oliveyards, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the corn, the wine, and the oil, that ye exact of them."

Nehemiah 5:12 — "Then said they, We will restore them, and will require nothing of them; so will we do as thou sayest. Then I called the priests, and took an oath of them, that they should do according to this promise."

Modern Corruption

The flood dates are dismissed as invented precision, and the usury reform of Nehemiah 5 is treated as an economic policy rather than a covenant obligation.

expand to see more

Genesis 7 and 8 give the flood a calendar: the seventeenth day of the second month of Noah's six hundredth year for the beginning, the first day of the first month of his six hundred and first for the drying, the twenty-seventh day of the second month for the earth being dry. Critical readings treat this precision as a literary device of a later editor, and the whole narrative as a reworked Mesopotamian flood story. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and a historical worldwide flood, and observes that our Lord treated Noah's days as fact and as the pattern of His own coming, and that Peter twice grounds doctrine on the historicity of the ark and the eight souls saved by water.

Nehemiah 5 is more often skipped than denied, which is its own kind of loss. The nobles were doing something legal by every commercial standard of the ancient world and forbidden by the law of Moses, which prohibited taking usury of a brother. Nehemiah's argument is not economic efficiency but covenant identity — ought ye not to walk in the fear of our God because of the reproach of the heathen our enemies? — and he adds that he and his servants had lent money and corn and would likewise leave off. He required nothing of others that he had not first done himself, which is why the assembly said amen and praised the LORD.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew meah, a hundred — Genesis 8:13; meath ha-keseph, the hundredth of the money — Nehemiah 5:11; neshek, usury, literally a bite.

expand to see more

Hebrew meah — a hundred; the numeral behind both uses.

Hebrew meath ha-keseph — “the hundredth of the money”; Nehemiah 5:11, understood as the monthly rate.

Hebrew neshek — usury, literally a bite; the word of the Mosaic prohibition, Exodus 22:25.

Hebrew mashsha — a loan or exaction; Nehemiah 5:7, the charge against the nobles.

Old English hundred, from hund and raed, a reckoning — the source of the English word.

Usage

"“In the six hundredth and first year, in the first month, the first day” — the flood dated by a man's years."

"“Also the hundredth part of the money… that ye exact of them” — the interest restored."

"“I called the priests, and took an oath of them” — Nehemiah did not trust the promise alone."
